rounds.q: Most sea stars have how many arms?
rounds.why: Five is the classic, but some species have 20 or more. Australia’s crown-of-thorns starfish can have over 20.

rounds.q: Owls swallow small prey whole, then cough up the bones and fur as…
rounds.why: Scientists pull owl pellets apart to see exactly what the owl had for dinner.

rounds.q: Dogs see the world mostly in…
rounds.why: Dogs have two kinds of colour cone, not three. Red and green look much the same to them.

rounds.q: Many frogs have webbed back feet. What are they best for?
rounds.why: Webbing turns each kick into a paddle stroke.

rounds.q: Rabbits’ and rodents’ front teeth never stop…
rounds.why: They grow all their lives and are worn down by gnawing. That’s why rats and mice chew everything.

rounds.q: A giraffe’s heart weighs about…
rounds.why: About 11 kg, with very thick walls. It has to push blood about two metres up the neck to the brain.

rounds.q: A turtle’s shell is…
rounds.answer: Bone, fused to its ribs and spine
wrong: A separate case it can leave
rounds.why: The shell is part of the skeleton. A turtle can no more leave its shell than you can leave your ribcage.

rounds.q: An earthworm has five pairs of…
rounds.why: Five pairs of muscly loops near the front squeeze blood along. Often called its ten ‘hearts’.

rounds.q: Which animal has three hearts and blue blood?
rounds.why: Two hearts pump blood through the gills, one pumps it round the body. Crabs have blue blood but just one heart. The first permanent artificial heart was fitted on this day in 1982.

rounds.q: Name the yellow lump on the back leg.
rounds.why: Bees pack pollen into a hair-fringed hollow on each back leg to carry it home.

rounds.q: How many toes does an owl have on each foot?
rounds.answer: Four, and one can swivel backwards
rounds.why: Owls can grip with two toes forward and two back, or three forward and one back.

rounds.q: A flamingo’s ‘backwards knee’ is actually its…
rounds.why: The real knee is hidden up under the feathers. The joint you see bend is the ankle.

rounds.q: How many compartments does a cow’s stomach have?
rounds.why: Rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Grass takes a long journey.

rounds.q: Geckos climb glass using…
rounds.answer: Millions of tiny hairs on their toes
rounds.why: Each toe pad carries millions of microscopic hairs that cling to surfaces with weak molecular forces. No glue involved.

rounds.q: A giant panda grips bamboo with a ‘thumb’ that is really…
wrong: A sixth finger with a nail
rounds.why: Pandas’ real thumbs are busy being normal paw digits. Evolution improvised with a wrist bone.

rounds.q: The highlighted openings are the owl’s ears. Why is one higher?
rounds.answer: To pinpoint sounds up and down
rounds.why: In owls like the barn owl, lopsided ears let them locate a mouse in total darkness.

rounds.q: Why can’t crocodiles stick their tongues out?
rounds.answer: A membrane holds it to the floor of the mouth
rounds.why: The tongue is tied down. A flap at the back of the throat seals out water instead.

rounds.q: Sea stars have no blood. What moves around inside instead?
rounds.why: A water-filled plumbing system powers the tube feet and moves things around.

rounds.q: A cheetah’s claws…
rounds.why: Always half out, they work like running spikes for grip at top speed.

rounds.q: Why does a cheetah have such a long tail?
rounds.answer: To steer and balance in sharp turns
rounds.why: At full speed the tail works like a rudder, so the cheetah can swerve after a zig-zagging gazelle.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted organ.
rounds.why: The ink sac squirts a dark cloud through the siphon, a smokescreen for a quick escape.

rounds.q: Roughly what share of an octopus’s neurons are in its arms?
rounds.why: Each arm can taste, feel and react with surprising independence. Group project energy.

rounds.q: A narwhal’s tusk is…
rounds.why: It’s a long spiral tooth, usually the left one, growing through the upper lip.

rounds.q: Dung beetles roll their balls in a straight line at night by…
wrong: Following the scent of other beetles
rounds.why: South African experiments found they use the glow of the Milky Way to keep their bearings. In a planetarium, too.

rounds.q: Earthworms breathe through their…
rounds.why: Oxygen soaks in through damp skin. That’s why worms come up when soil floods: they need air.

rounds.q: In the dark Arctic winter, reindeer eyes change colour from gold to…
rounds.why: A reflective layer at the back of the eye shifts colour, which helps scatter light in the long winter dark.

rounds.q: Mantis shrimp eyes have about how many types of colour receptor?
rounds.why: We have three. They have about 12, but oddly don’t seem better at telling colours apart.

rounds.q: The backward-facing spines on a cat’s tongue are hollow. Why?
rounds.answer: To wick saliva deep into fur
rounds.why: Scoop-shaped tips soak up saliva and deliver it to the skin during grooming.

rounds.q: What is this small highlighted slit at the base of the ear for?
rounds.why: Henry’s pocket may help with hearing high-pitched sounds or let the ear fold. Science shrugs.

rounds.q: Reindeer make a clicking sound as they walk. What makes it?
rounds.answer: A tendon slipping over a bone in the foot
rounds.why: The clicks help a herd stay together in snowstorms and the dark. Finns and Sámi herders know the sound well.

rounds.q: Octopuses zoom away by squirting water out of this. It works like a…
rounds.why: Jet propulsion: suck water into the mantle, squeeze it out of the siphon, shoot off backwards.

rounds.q: Common swifts can stay in the air without landing for about…
rounds.why: Tracking showed some swifts flew for about 10 months straight, eating and even napping on the wing.

rounds.q: Which bird can dive at more than 300 km/h?
rounds.why: In a hunting dive a peregrine is the fastest animal on Earth.

rounds.q: Which of these birds can’t fly?
rounds.why: Emus have tiny wings and run instead, up to about 50 km/h.

rounds.q: How does a hummingbird save energy overnight?
rounds.answer: It drops into a deep, cold sleep
wrong: It sleeps in a group hug
rounds.why: In torpor its heart rate and body temperature plunge, then it warms back up by morning.

rounds.q: In bright light, a cat’s pupils shrink to…
rounds.why: Slits can close down much further than round pupils, handy for an animal that hunts at dawn, dusk and night.

rounds.q: Koalas have something surprisingly like ours. What?
rounds.why: Koala fingerprints are so like human ones that even under a microscope they’re hard to tell apart.

rounds.q: Clownfish are all born…
rounds.why: The biggest fish in a group is the female. If she disappears, the top male changes to take her place.

rounds.q: In seahorses, who carries the eggs until they hatch?
rounds.why: Mum puts the eggs in dad’s pouch, and he carries them until the babies pop out.

rounds.q: How do camels keep out blowing sand?
wrong: They hide their head in their hump
rounds.why: Slit-like nostrils seal shut, and two rows of long eyelashes guard the eyes.

rounds.q: An elephant’s trunk has no bones but about how many muscle bundles?
rounds.why: Usually put at around 40,000 muscle units, which is why a trunk can pick up a peanut or rip down a branch.

rounds.q: Bird lungs work differently from ours. Air flows…
wrong: In and out of two balloons
rounds.why: Air sacs push air one way through stiff lungs, so birds get fresh air on the way in and out.

rounds.q: Why are a beaver’s front teeth orange?
rounds.why: Iron makes the enamel tougher, perfect for felling trees.

rounds.q: How many eyes does a box jellyfish have?
rounds.why: Four clusters of six eyes, some of them with lenses. Not bad for an animal without a brain.

rounds.q: A brown pelican’s throat pouch can hold about…
rounds.why: Roughly three US gallons. It scoops, drains the water out, then swallows the fish.

rounds.q: How many eyes does a honeybee have in total?
rounds.why: Two compound eyes for seeing and three simple eyes on top for sensing light.

rounds.q: Nobel Prize winner Karl von Frisch showed how honeybees tell each other where food is. They…
rounds.why: The ‘waggle dance’ points the way and shows how far. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.

rounds.q: Each alligator tooth can be replaced up to about…
rounds.why: A spare tooth waits under each one, ready to move in.

rounds.q: Dragonflies catch roughly what share of the prey they chase?
rounds.why: They predict where the prey is heading and fly to intercept. Among the best hunters on Earth.

rounds.q: Polar bear hairs are actually…
rounds.why: The clear hairs scatter light, so the coat looks white. The skin underneath is black.

rounds.q: A snow leopard’s long, thick tail is used as…
rounds.answer: A balance pole and a scarf
rounds.why: It helps it balance on steep rock and wraps around its face when it sleeps in the cold.

rounds.q: Bar-headed geese fly on migration over which mountains?
rounds.why: Their blood grabs oxygen extra tightly, so they cope with air that would leave us gasping. Today is International Mountain Day.

rounds.q: Mountain goats grip cliffs with hooves that have…
rounds.answer: Rubbery pads inside a hard rim
rounds.why: The hard rim digs in and the soft pad grips, like a climbing shoe.

rounds.q: Alpacas and llamas, from the Andes, have no top front teeth. Instead they have a…
rounds.why: Bottom teeth press grass against the tough pad, a bit like a cow.

rounds.q: Sea cucumbers breathe through their…
rounds.why: They pump water in and out of the rear end to feed branching ‘respiratory trees’ inside.

rounds.q: Elephant tusks keep growing…
rounds.why: Tusks are giant incisor teeth that keep growing, which is why old elephants can have very long ones.

rounds.q: A woodpecker’s long tongue, when tucked away…
rounds.why: The tongue bones loop round the back of the skull and may help cushion all that hammering.

rounds.q: How many toes does an ostrich have on each foot?
rounds.why: The only bird with just two toes. The big one has a thick claw and does most of the work.

rounds.q: Zebra stripes seem to mainly…
rounds.why: In tests in Kenya and elsewhere, flies struggled to land on stripes. Horses in striped coats got fewer landings too.

rounds.q: A snail’s teeth are found…
rounds.why: The radula is a rasping ribbon with thousands of microscopic teeth.

rounds.q: In basking sharks, the liver can be about what share of body weight?
rounds.why: Up to around 20 to 25%. Oil is lighter than water, so it works like a built-in float.

rounds.q: A horse’s hoof is really one giant…
rounds.why: Horses walk on the tip of one middle toe. The hoof is a supersized toenail.

rounds.q: What’s special about the hair on a sloth?
rounds.why: Grooves in the hairs hold algae, which may give a greenish camouflage. Sloth fur also grows from belly to back, so rain runs off when they hang upside down.

rounds.q: About how many whiskers does a cat have on its muzzle in total?
rounds.why: Usually 12 a side, in four rows. The top two rows can move independently of the bottom two.

rounds.q: Flies balance in flight using tiny knobs where a second pair of wings would be. What are they called?
rounds.why: Halteres beat like tiny gyroscopes and help a fly sense turns. It’s why flies are so hard to swat.

rounds.q: An octopus squirts ink mainly to…
rounds.why: A dark cloud, sometimes shaped roughly like an octopus, while the real one jets away.

rounds.q: A European leech bites with how many jaws?
rounds.why: Three tiny saw-like jaws, each with rows of teeth.

rounds.q: Snakes swallow huge meals because their lower jaw…
rounds.answer: Has two halves that stretch apart
rounds.why: The two halves aren’t fused at the chin, and stretchy tissue lets them spread wide. They don’t ‘unhinge’.

rounds.q: Which animal has the largest eyes of any land mammal?
rounds.why: Big eyes on the sides of the head give horses an almost all-round view.

rounds.q: Which mosquitoes bite?
rounds.why: Females need a meal of blood to make eggs. Males just drink nectar.

rounds.q: The word ‘octopus’ comes from Greek for…
rounds.why: Okto (eight) plus pous (foot). Linguists argue about the plural, too: octopuses is fine.

rounds.q: ‘Rhinoceros’ comes from Greek words meaning…
rounds.why: Rhino (nose) plus keras (horn).

rounds.q: ‘Hippopotamus’ comes from Greek for…
rounds.why: Hippos (horse) plus potamos (river). Their closest living relatives are actually whales.

rounds.q: ‘Porcupine’ comes from old words meaning…
rounds.why: From Old French porc espin, from Latin for pig and spine.

rounds.q: The giraffe’s scientific name, camelopardalis, says people once thought it was a cross between…
rounds.why: Long neck like a camel, spots like a leopard. The name stuck.

rounds.q: How many muscles move each cat ear?
rounds.why: That’s why cats can swivel each ear separately towards a sound.

rounds.q: Which animal can hear the highest-pitched sounds known?
rounds.why: It can pick up sounds up to about 300 kHz, far higher than bats can squeak. Likely an arms race with bats.

rounds.q: Where are a grasshopper’s ears?
rounds.why: Many grasshoppers have an eardrum on each side of the first belly segment.

rounds.q: Most bats find food in the dark using…
rounds.why: Echolocation: they shout, mostly too high for us to hear, then listen for what bounces back.

rounds.q: Snakes have no outer ears. How do they pick up sound?
rounds.why: Their jaw bones pass ground vibrations, and some low airborne sounds, to the inner ear.

rounds.q: Flying fish don’t flap. They ‘fly’ by…
wrong: Flapping their tails in the air
rounds.why: They burst out of the water and glide, sometimes for dozens of metres, to escape predators.

rounds.q: Many bird bones are hollow inside. What fills them?
rounds.why: Air sacs from the lungs reach into some bones, making them light and part of the breathing system. Humans first flew a plane on this day in 1903.

rounds.q: Albatrosses can glide for hours partly thanks to…
rounds.answer: A shoulder lock that holds the wings out
rounds.why: With wings locked out, they barely spend energy, so they can travel huge distances over the ocean.

rounds.q: In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania. About how far?
rounds.why: About 13,560 km in 11 days without landing, a world record for nonstop bird flight.

rounds.q: Ducks stand on ice without freezing their feet thanks to…
rounds.answer: Warm and cold blood vessels swapping heat
wrong: Wearing a layer of fat on their toes
rounds.why: Warm blood heading down warms the cold blood coming up, so little heat is lost through the feet.

rounds.q: Before a huge migration, bar-tailed godwits shrink their…
rounds.why: They shrink digestive organs they won’t need in flight and bulk up on fuel and flight muscle.

rounds.q: Arctic terns travel about how far each year?
rounds.why: Pole to pole and back. Over a lifetime that’s like flying to the Moon and back about three times.

rounds.q: Salmon find their way back to the river where they hatched mainly by…
rounds.why: Each river has its own scent mix, and young salmon memorise it.

rounds.q: Monarch butterflies keep their migration on course using the sun and…
rounds.answer: A body clock in their antennae
rounds.why: The antennae help keep time, so they can correct for the sun moving across the sky.

rounds.q: Sea turtles cross oceans and find their home beach partly by sensing…
rounds.why: Each stretch of coast has its own magnetic ‘signature’ that turtles seem to remember.

rounds.q: The floppy red skin hanging over a turkey’s beak is called the…
rounds.why: Male turkeys can stretch the snood longer when showing off. The wattle is the dangly bit under the chin.

rounds.q: Geese don’t have teeth, but the edges of their bill have tooth-like ridges called…
rounds.why: Serrated bill edges help grip and tear grass. They can give a nasty pinch.

rounds.q: Which frog has see-through belly skin, so you can see its insides?
rounds.why: Some glass frogs even hide their blood in their liver while sleeping, turning almost fully see-through.

rounds.q: In many birds, the crop is a pouch for…
rounds.why: A stretchy bulge in the throat lets birds grab lots of food fast, then digest later.

rounds.q: A male turkey’s bare head can change colour between…
rounds.why: Blood flow changes the colour with mood. Bright red usually means he’s fired up.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted sieve-like plate.
rounds.why: It lets seawater into the sea star’s plumbing that powers its tube feet.

rounds.q: Which mammal can have up to 10 neck vertebrae?
rounds.why: Most mammals have seven. Three-toed sloths have extra, manatees and two-toed sloths fewer.

rounds.q: A shark’s tail has a bigger upper lobe. What does that do?
rounds.answer: Gives lift as well as push
rounds.why: The lopsided tail pushes the shark forwards and slightly up, which helps without a swim bladder.

rounds.q: Octopuses and jellyfish keep track of up and down using little balance organs called…
rounds.why: A tiny stone rolls inside a fluid-filled sac lined with sensors, telling the animal which way is down.

rounds.q: The furry gliding skin of a sugar glider is called the…
rounds.why: It stretches from wrist to ankle, so the glider can sail up to about 50 metres between trees.

rounds.q: The colossal squid’s eye is about the size of a…
rounds.why: About 27 cm across, the largest eye known in the animal kingdom.

rounds.q: Sloths can slow their heart and hold their breath for up to about…
rounds.why: Longer than dolphins can. Handy for a surprisingly good swimmer.

rounds.q: Which animal can sleep up to about 20 hours a day?
rounds.why: Gum leaves are low in energy, so koalas save energy by resting most of the day.

rounds.q: A cat’s purr is made by…
rounds.why: Muscles and tissues in the voice box vibrate as the cat breathes in and out.

rounds.q: The tallest animal alive is the…
rounds.why: Males can reach about 5.5 metres. Their legs alone are taller than many people.

rounds.q: Centipedes always have an odd number of…
rounds.why: Anywhere from 15 to 191 pairs, but always odd. So no centipede has exactly 100 legs.

rounds.q: Honeybees build honeycomb cells in what shape?
rounds.why: Hexagons fit together with no gaps and use the least wax for the space.

rounds.q: Most snail shells coil which way?
rounds.why: About 9 in 10 snail species coil to the right. Left-coiling snails struggle to find mates.

rounds.q: An octopus has roughly how many suckers across all eight arms?
rounds.why: A common octopus has a couple of hundred on each arm. Each one can grip, feel and taste.

rounds.q: Crabs and lobsters belong to a group named for having ten…
rounds.why: Decapods: ‘deca’ means ten. The front pair is often the big claws.

rounds.q: Nine-banded armadillos almost always give birth to…
rounds.why: One fertilised egg splits into four, so all four pups are identical.

rounds.q: What can a sea cucumber push out of its body and regrow?
rounds.why: Threatened, some throw out their insides to distract predators, then regrow them in weeks.

rounds.q: Cut certain flatworms into pieces and each piece can…
rounds.answer: Grow into a whole new worm
wrong: Swim off as half a worm
rounds.why: Planarian flatworms are regeneration champions. Even a tiny fragment can rebuild a head.

rounds.q: Marmoset monkeys usually give birth to…
rounds.why: Twins are the norm, and dads and older siblings do much of the carrying.

rounds.q: A newborn giraffe’s first moment is a drop of about…
rounds.why: Mums give birth standing up. The calf is usually standing within an hour.

rounds.q: Reindeer noses keep the cold out thanks to…
rounds.answer: A dense network of tiny blood vessels
wrong: Thick fur inside the nostrils only
rounds.why: Lots of blood flow warms the air they breathe in. A red nose isn’t just for Rudolph.

rounds.q: Reindeer are the only deer where…
rounds.why: Females keep theirs through winter, so Santa’s team, still antlered in December, may be mostly girls.

rounds.q: During winter hibernation, black bears can go months without…
rounds.answer: Eating, drinking or going to the toilet
rounds.why: They live off stored fat and recycle waste. No midnight snacks.

rounds.q: One gulp from a feeding blue whale can take in water and krill roughly equal to…
rounds.why: Its pleated throat balloons out, then it pushes the water out through its baleen and keeps the krill.

rounds.q: Penguins drink seawater and get rid of the extra salt through…
rounds.why: The salt gland drips salty liquid out through the beak. Penguins often look like they have a runny nose.

rounds.q: Chameleons change colour mainly by…
rounds.answer: Rearranging tiny crystals in their skin
rounds.why: Layers of nanocrystals shift spacing, changing which colours of light bounce back.

rounds.q: Bats can hang upside down while asleep without effort because…
rounds.answer: Their weight pulls tendons that lock the toes shut
wrong: They hold on with their teeth
rounds.why: Gravity does the work. They actually have to use muscle to let go.

rounds.q: Peacock feather colours come from…
rounds.why: Structural colour, like a soap bubble: change the angle and the colour shifts.

rounds.q: Which of these animals can see ultraviolet light, invisible to us?
rounds.why: In snowy Arctic light, UV vision makes urine, lichen and wolves stand out against the snow.

rounds.q: Cuttlefish are colour-change masters, but they are probably…
rounds.why: They have just one type of light sensor in their eyes. How they match colours is still a puzzle.

rounds.q: In 2020, scientists shone ultraviolet light on museum platypus specimens. What did the fur do?
rounds.why: Found in 2020 with museum specimens. Nobody is sure if it does anything useful.

rounds.q: Fireflies make light that gives off almost no…
rounds.why: A chemical reaction makes ‘cold light’. Nearly all the energy goes into glow.

rounds.q: The glow-worms in Australian and New Zealand caves are actually…
rounds.why: They’re young fungus gnats. They dangle sticky threads to catch insects drawn to the glow.

rounds.q: An anglerfish’s glowing lure gets its light from…
rounds.why: Bacteria living in the lure make the light. The fish just provides a home.

rounds.q: The blue sparkle in waves at night usually comes from…
rounds.answer: Tiny plankton that glow when disturbed
rounds.why: Single-celled algae flash when the water moves, so breaking waves light up.

rounds.q: Pigeons feed their chicks a ‘milk’ made in their…
rounds.why: Both parents make crop milk, a rich, cheesy paste. Flamingos and male emperor penguins make something similar.

rounds.q: A hummingbird’s heart can beat more than ___ times a minute.
rounds.why: Over 1,200 beats a minute in flight. At night it can slow right down to save energy.

rounds.q: Elephants have a hidden ‘sixth toe’ in each foot. What is it?
rounds.answer: A rod of cartilage and bone
rounds.why: This ‘predigit’ props up the foot’s fatty heel pad, a bit like a hidden high heel.

rounds.q: How many neck vertebrae does a manatee have?
rounds.why: Manatees are rare mammals with fewer than seven. They can’t turn their heads much.

rounds.q: A snake flicks its tongue, then touches the tips to a scent organ in the roof of its mouth called…
rounds.why: Also called the vomeronasal organ. The forked tongue helps tell which side a smell is coming from.

rounds.q: Weight for weight, spider silk can be stronger than…
rounds.why: Spider-Man’s writers didn’t make that up. Some silks are also stretchier than nylon.

rounds.q: Which tiny animal survived 10 days exposed to outer space?
rounds.why: In 2007, ‘water bears’ rode on a satellite outside, and some survived. Superhero material.

rounds.q: A mantis shrimp’s punch is so fast it makes the water…
rounds.answer: Form bubbles that collapse with a flash
rounds.why: The strike is so quick that collapsing bubbles hit prey a second time and give off a tiny flash of light.

rounds.q: Besides colour, an octopus can instantly change its…
rounds.why: Little bumps rise up to mimic rocks, coral or seaweed. Camouflage superpower.

rounds.q: Which animal has the strongest bite ever measured?
rounds.why: A big saltie clamped down with over 16,000 newtons in tests, the most measured for a living animal.

rounds.q: Pufferfish puff up by gulping…
rounds.why: They swallow water fast, ballooning to several times their size. Many are also very poisonous.

rounds.q: When snakes shed their skin, it usually comes off…
rounds.answer: In one piece, often inside out
rounds.why: It peels back from the lips like a sock. Even the clear eye scales come off.

rounds.q: Sea cucumbers can switch their body from firm to…
rounds.why: Special stretchy tissue lets them stiffen up or go limp in seconds, handy for squeezing into cracks.

rounds.q: Kangaroo leg tendons work like rubber bands: they…
rounds.why: Stretchy tendons spring back, so a fast hop costs a kangaroo very little extra energy.

rounds.q: Hamsters carry food home in…
rounds.why: The pouches stretch back to their shoulders. ‘Hamstern’ in German means to hoard.

rounds.q: What do the two smaller highlighted hearts do?
rounds.why: They’re branchial hearts. The bigger one in the middle then sends that oxygen-rich blood around the body.

rounds.q: Name the highlighted pores on the shark’s snout.
rounds.why: Named after Stefano Lorenzini, who described them in 1678. They sense electric fields.

rounds.q: A few stiff hairs grow near this highlighted pad. What are they called?
rounds.why: Mystacial are the muzzle ones, superciliary over the eyes and genal on the cheeks. Carpal whiskers sense wriggling prey.

rounds.q: Which tongue papillae give a cat’s tongue its hollow, scoop-tipped spines?
rounds.why: Filiform papillae are the rough, backward-hooked ones. Their hollow tips wick saliva into the fur.

rounds.q: What is a honeybee’s pollen basket properly called?
rounds.why: A scopa is the pollen brush of many solitary bees, a tegula covers the wing base and a pulvillus is a foot pad.

rounds.q: Greenland sharks may live for about…
rounds.why: Eye-lens dating in 2016 suggested the oldest was about 400. Some alive today may have been born before Isaac Newton.

rounds.q: Which animal can turn itself back into a baby stage?
rounds.why: Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into a young polyp and start life again. New year, new jellyfish.

rounds.q: Dogs often panic at fireworks partly because they can hear…
rounds.why: Dogs hear higher pitches than we do, and loud bangs come with no warning.

rounds.q: To grow bigger, lobsters…
rounds.why: They wriggle out, puff up with water and wait for a new, larger shell to harden.

rounds.q: In summer, a worker honeybee lives about…
rounds.why: They wear themselves out foraging. Winter workers and queens live much longer.
